video_title: Jamie Coutts: The 3 Crypto Tokens I'm Holding This Bull Cycle
gist: Real Vision analyst Jamie Coutts argues Bitcoin is in a bear market driven by debt rising faster than global liquidity — not by Michael Saylor's Strategy, which he calls a symptom amplified by an already-weak tape — and says he is holding his highest cash position in a long time, waiting for a weekly momentum shift plus a dollar/real-yield rollover before adding risk. His constructive 12-month crypto thesis rests on tokenization plus AI-agent block-space demand meeting newly disciplined tokenomics, with NEAR's intents protocol (100% of intents fees to buybacks) as his clearest single-name expression. Note: despite the title's '3 tokens' framing, he never enumerates a three-token portfolio — he discusses NEAR bullishly, Ethereum as attractive but not yet bought, and Zcash as a position he currently does NOT hold.

insights.claim: Jamie Coutts argues Bitcoin did not top because of Micro Strategy — the cycle top was driven by long-term holder selling that peaked in Q3 of last year, and Saylor's problems are only a focal point because the market was already in a bear market.
insights.speaker: Jamie Coutts
insights.so_what: Traders shorting Bitcoin purely on Strategy-unwind headlines are trading a second-order symptom; the actual variable to track is aggregate demand and long-term holder distribution.
insights.quote: it wouldn't be such a focal point for the market if we weren't in a bare market

insights.claim: Coutts frames Micro Strategy's failure mode as over-dosing a fundamentally sound idea: putting Bitcoin on the balance sheet makes sense, but layering exotic financial-engineering structures exceeds the market's finite capacity to absorb those products at any one time.
insights.speaker: Jamie Coutts
insights.so_what: A capacity-limit lens on Bitcoin treasury companies: monitor the market's appetite for each new preferred/convertible structure as the leading indicator of DAT stress, not the BTC price alone.
insights.quote: the dosage determines the poison, right?

insights.claim: Coutts says Strategy's newly announced capital management program does solidify the company's base but comes at Bitcoin's expense, because over time Saylor will use the Bitcoin stack to defend the vehicles he has built.
insights.speaker: Jamie Coutts
insights.so_what: Implies a persistent structural BTC supply overhang from the largest corporate holder — a reason to expect capped rallies even as MSTR equity stabilizes.

insights.claim: The host draws a direct parallel between Strategy's STRC math and crypto tokenomics: Bitcoin must appreciate faster than STRC's cost for Saylor's model to be self-sustaining, exactly as a protocol with 40-50% annual unlocks must grow demand faster than its own supply schedule.
insights.speaker: host (Michael)
insights.so_what: A single screening test applicable to both DATs and tokens: is the growth rate of demand outrunning the mandated growth rate of supply/liabilities?

themes.theme: Anatomy of the Q3 cycle top

insights.claim: Coutts's Bitcoin cycle risk model flagged a top in Q3 of last year, though he personally read it as a 30-40% correction rather than the end-of-cycle top it turned out to be.
insights.speaker: Jamie Coutts
insights.so_what: The model was right while its author's discretionary overlay was wrong — an argument for weighting systematic cycle-risk signals over narrative when they conflict.

insights.claim: Coutts identifies four confluent ingredients behind the Bitcoin top: long-term holder selling, an explosion in leverage measured as open interest relative to market cap, the Binance episode that exposed crypto's fragile market structure, and Q4 fiscal tightening from the US government shutdown alongside ongoing Fed QT.
insights.speaker: Jamie Coutts
insights.so_what: A reusable four-factor top checklist — open interest / market cap is the specific leverage ratio he watches for topping signals.

insights.claim: Coutts believes the market is in a bottoming window but explicitly not finished with the downside, and that the liquidity relief needed for a durable low most likely arrives next year rather than this year.
insights.speaker: Jamie Coutts
insights.so_what: Sets a timeline: he is positioning for a multi-quarter base, not an imminent V-shaped recovery — argues for staged accumulation rather than a single bid.

insights.claim: Coutts expects the next sharp leg down in Bitcoin to be a capitulation low and a great buying opportunity, but insists on waiting for a long-term momentum indicator to confirm a supply/demand regime change rather than trying to pick the bottom.
insights.speaker: Jamie Coutts
insights.so_what: Concrete execution rule: buy the confirmed momentum turn after capitulation, not the capitulation itself.
insights.quote: don't try and pick the bottom

insights.claim: Coutts distinguishes a recoverable Bitcoin crash from a thesis-breaking one: proof of a functioning quantum computer or dormant Satoshi-era coins moving on chain would be a long-repair problem, which is why he sees urgency in Bitcoin upgrading to quantum resistance.
insights.speaker: Jamie Coutts
insights.so_what: Defines the one tail risk that would invalidate rather than discount the Bitcoin thesis — worth monitoring old-coin movement as a live kill-signal.

insights.claim: The host notes Bitcoin has just lost the 200-week moving average, an indicator that has marked every bottoming process except 2022, when it broke down due to the FTX collapse and the Luna implosion.
insights.speaker: host (Michael)
insights.so_what: A specific, checkable technical level: reclaiming the 200-week MA is the near-term bull/bear line for this cycle.

insights.claim: Coutts's core macro claim is that global liquidity aggregates are rising but debt is rising faster, which is why risk assets are not responding to headline liquidity growth.
insights.speaker: Jamie Coutts
insights.so_what: Reframes the popular 'M2 is expanding so buy Bitcoin' trade — the tradable variable is the debt-to-liquidity ratio, not liquidity in isolation.

insights.claim: Coutts lists the evidence that debt demand is overwhelming liquidity supply: the dollar breaking out of a year-long consolidation range, rising inflation expectations, and a bear flattening in which the short end rises relative to the long end.
insights.speaker: Jamie Coutts
insights.so_what: Three concrete confirmations to watch daily; their reversal is the entry trigger for risk assets.

insights.claim: Coutts argues a rising dollar with rising real yields has a built-in expiry date because it eventually breaks something, and the US government cannot tolerate a falling market since that destroys tax receipts and widens an already post-WWII-crisis-level deficit.
insights.speaker: Jamie Coutts
insights.so_what: The policy-put logic behind the debasement trade: pain is the mechanism that forces the liquidity response, so weakness now is a precondition for the eventual bid.

insights.claim: Coutts cites US net interest relative to GDP back at all-time highs above 3%, a level last seen in 1990 before the 1990s great moderation and budget-balancing effort, with forecasts pointing materially higher.
insights.speaker: Jamie Coutts
insights.so_what: Quantifies the fiscal constraint that ultimately caps how high yields can go before a liquidity program becomes politically forced.
insights.quote: net interest relative to GDP is back at all-time highs. It was it's over 3%

insights.claim: Coutts identifies next year as the biggest net differential in US issuance, with a large slug of low-coupon COVID-era debt resetting at much higher rates — resolvable only through higher yields or some form of liquidity program.
insights.speaker: Jamie Coutts
insights.so_what: Puts a calendar on the debasement trade: the refi wall next year is the forcing function for the liquidity pivot he is waiting to buy.

insights.claim: Coutts expects the dollar to rally further toward roughly 104, an environment in which risk assets will not do well.
insights.speaker: Jamie Coutts
insights.so_what: A specific level to trade against: DXY ~104 is his implied pain threshold, and its rollover is a buy signal for crypto.
insights.quote: I think it's going to sort of 104 to be perfectly honest in that environment risk assets won't do well

insights.claim: Coutts suspects Kevin Walsh will not go on a rate-hike spree because inflation data has already rolled over and the market is doing the tightening for him, while his effective mandate from Trump is to sustain economic growth into an election.
insights.speaker: Jamie Coutts
insights.so_what: Fades the hawkish read of the first Walsh presentation — if he is right, rate-hike-driven risk-asset selling is an overreaction to be faded.
insights.quote: I suspect that Walsh is letting the market tighten um for him so he doesn't actually have to raise rates

themes.theme: The new credit channel: why liquidity stopped reaching crypto

insights.claim: Coutts splits monetary history into two eras: 2008-2021/22 central-bank QE, which inflated asset prices without pushing credit into the real economy, and a post-2022 'Treasury QE' era in which liquidity reaches the real economy through bank-intermediated credit.
insights.speaker: Jamie Coutts
insights.so_what: Explains the regime change directly: the channel that used to pump debasement assets like gold and Bitcoin now pumps corporate earnings instead.

insights.claim: Coutts attributes Bitcoin's broken correlation with global liquidity to changed bank capital adequacy rules under the current administration that let banks buy and lever US government debt, routing new liquidity into real-economy credit consumed largely by AI hyperscalers rather than into crypto.
insights.speaker: Jamie Coutts
insights.so_what: The mechanistic explanation for why the M2-Bitcoin correlation broke down around late 2025 — the correlation returns only when the credit channel stops favouring AI capex.
insights.quote: capital flows to where it's treated best

insights.claim: Coutts identifies three channels draining liquidity from markets: new equity listings/IPOs, investment-grade debt issuance by hyperscalers, and US government issuance as the largest by far.
insights.speaker: Jamie Coutts
insights.so_what: A liquidity-demand scorecard for timing risk-asset exposure; the government leg dominates and peaks next year.

insights.claim: Coutts flags that hyperscalers represent 20-30% of total market buybacks, so their pivot from free-cash-flow buybacks into capex plus debt issuance is a double liquidity withdrawal from equity markets.
insights.speaker: Jamie Coutts
insights.so_what: Quantifies a rarely-modelled drag on US equities: the marginal buyback bid shrinks exactly as new IG supply arrives.

insights.claim: Coutts would not buy hyperscalers now given his liquidity outlook and notes they are already underperforming the market, but expects better prices within roughly six months; he carves out Tesla as different because of a more diversified revenue base and a coming robotics theme it is not yet monetizing.
insights.speaker: Jamie Coutts
insights.so_what: An explicit six-month waiting window on mega-cap AI, with robotics flagged as the next thematic rotation after compute and energy.

themes.theme: AI plateau, agentic commerce and crypto as the agent substrate

insights.claim: Coutts believes the apparent plateau in frontier model capability is temporary and that recursive self-improvement means the next major breakthrough is not far away, putting markets on the cusp of the financialization of AI.
insights.speaker: Jamie Coutts
insights.so_what: If right, the current 'diminishing returns' narrative is a buying window for the next AI-driven leg rather than evidence of a bubble top.

insights.claim: Coutts suspects publicly released models are dumbed-down versions of far more capable internal systems being held back while risk mitigations are worked out, and says Anthropic is playing games to build a regulatory moat, which he finds concerning.
insights.speaker: Jamie Coutts
insights.so_what: A regulatory-capture read on AI: incumbents lobbying for rules would raise barriers and compress the opportunity set for challengers and open-source models.
insights.quote: some games being played by Anthropic to try and create a regulatory moat, which I find concerning

insights.claim: Coutts's 12-month playbook is that two themes converge to drive on-chain demand — regulatory clarity/tokenization and AI agents — with agentic commerce arriving as analysts give their agents wallets and semi-autonomous spending authority for paid API calls.
insights.speaker: Jamie Coutts
insights.so_what: Gives a falsifiable 12-month horizon and a specific verification method: watch on-chain data for agent activity, which currently shows none.

insights.claim: Coutts argues US crypto market-structure clarity is far less important than consensus thinks — Polymarket odds are around 39% — because DTCC is proceeding with a second-half pilot for tokenized Russell 1000 stocks and ETFs and the SEC has effectively green-lit progress without legislation.
insights.speaker: Jamie Coutts
insights.so_what: A failed clarity bill would be a headline-driven dip to buy, since the institutional tokenization rails are being laid regardless.

insights.claim: Coutts says the government wants tokenization because digitalizing markets helps it find buyers for its debt, tying the tokenization push directly back to the Treasury's financing problem — citing Bessent speaking publicly on blockchain and tokenization.
insights.speaker: Jamie Coutts
insights.so_what: Explains why policy support for tokenization should prove durable and bipartisan-proof: it serves the debt-funding imperative.

insights.claim: Coutts positions Real Vision's portfolio primarily in L1s on the logic that L1s are the substrate for the agentic era, and that rising block-space demand is highly correlated with the price of the underlying tokens.
insights.speaker: Jamie Coutts
insights.so_what: A stated portfolio construction: express the agentic-crypto thesis through L1 tokens rather than application tokens.

insights.claim: Coutts notes crypto reached a $3 trillion peak market cap on only around 20 million daily active users, and frames the upside as a step-function in participants — 100 million, then a billion — as AI expands the number of economic actors transacting on blockchains.
insights.speaker: Jamie Coutts
insights.so_what: A concrete valuation anchor: $3T per 20M DAUs sets the scaling arithmetic for the agent-driven bull case.
insights.quote: we got to three trillion at its high in total market cap for the crypto economy just with daily active users of about 20 million

themes.theme: Supply discipline and Ethereum's value-accrual problem

insights.claim: Coutts argues supply discipline in tokenomics will be the defining crypto theme of the next couple of years, and that if disciplined supply meets a genuine demand wave it would be the first time crypto has had both simultaneously.
insights.speaker: Jamie Coutts
insights.so_what: A screening mandate: rank tokens by supply schedule and value accrual first, narrative second — he explicitly changed his own mind on this.
insights.quote: like Hyperlid showed the way other protocols are starting to follow suit

insights.claim: Coutts explains that badly designed, insider-favourable tokenomics were built on an assumption of perpetually up-and-to-the-right demand, so when demand failed to arrive many fundamentally useful protocols were sunk by their own unlocks and inflation rates.
insights.speaker: Jamie Coutts
insights.so_what: Separates technology quality from token performance — a good protocol can still be an uninvestable token purely on supply mechanics.

insights.claim: Coutts attributes recent downtrend breakouts in several tokens primarily to tokenomics policy changes rather than to any improvement in usage, citing Jupiter as one of the best performers after a major tokenomics change several months ago.
insights.speaker: Jamie Coutts
insights.so_what: Actionable screen: monitor governance forums for tokenomics/buyback proposals as a leading indicator of relative outperformance in a bear tape.

insights.claim: Coutts says Ethereum already instituted strong supply discipline via EIP-1559 in 2021 and is therefore not part of the tokenomics problem, and that relative to its own activity history ETH is looking cheaper than it has ever been — though he is not buying at these levels given his short-term caution.
insights.speaker: Jamie Coutts
insights.so_what: A named analyst calling ETH historically cheap on an activity-relative basis while explicitly waiting for a macro trigger — sets up a watch-list entry rather than an immediate buy.
insights.quote: relative to where it's been in terms of its activity, it's actually looking cheaper than it's ever been

insights.claim: Coutts values L1s like Ethereum and Solana through a layered stack: validator/economic participation in security, fees as part of the security model, and application-layer activity, profitability, number of applications and the on-chain GDP they generate.
insights.speaker: Jamie Coutts
insights.so_what: A concrete four-layer valuation framework for L1 tokens that goes beyond price-to-fees.

insights.claim: Coutts argues the 2021 cycle ended not only on liquidity but because block-space congestion choked demand — gas going from $60 to $100 killed application-layer activity — which is why the last four years were spent scaling to abundant block space.
insights.speaker: Jamie Coutts
insights.so_what: Explains why abundant block space is now a demand precondition rather than a bearish oversupply — capacity is no longer the binding constraint.

insights.claim: Coutts's main criticism of Ethereum is that scaling via L2s stunted value accrual to the ETH token, when horizontal scaling and sharding — discussed in 2016-17 then dropped — were available, with NEAR as the best proof it can be done and done dynamically.
insights.speaker: Jamie Coutts
insights.so_what: The bear case on ETH is architectural, not demand-based; its offsetting moat is that Ethereum remains the liquidity center of gravity and the first stop for tokenization projects.

themes.theme: NEAR intents and the privacy-coin trade-off

insights.claim: Coutts's NEAR thesis is that its intents protocol solves crypto's long-standing interoperability problem in a self-custodial way, and that NEAR has already captured a large share of bridging/interoperability revenue within about a year of launching it.
insights.speaker: Jamie Coutts
insights.so_what: Frames NEAR as a cross-chain toll road rather than a competing L1 — a different risk profile from block-space-competition L1 bets.

insights.claim: Coutts highlights that NEAR routes 100% of intents fees into buybacks, calling it a great value accrual mechanism, and that intents now generate roughly 100,000 a day in fees versus roughly 1,000-2,000 a day for NEAR's underlying L1 on its best days.
insights.speaker: Jamie Coutts
insights.so_what: A ~50-100x step change in protocol revenue with a direct buyback link — the specific, checkable number underpinning the trade.

insights.claim: Coutts positions NEAR as non-rivalrous with Solana and Ethereum: it does not compete for L1 block-space demand but benefits from their growth because users want to transact across chains, with agentic commerce multiplying that activity.
insights.speaker: Jamie Coutts
insights.so_what: Makes NEAR a levered call on total crypto activity rather than a market-share bet — a way to own the sector's growth without picking the winning L1.
insights.quote: So NIA is not fighting for L1 block space demand like Soul and Ethereum is. It's benefiting from the increase in demand from Soul and Ethereum

insights.claim: Coutts explains the gap between NEAR's growing narrative and its ~50% price drawdown over two to three months: intents volume has flatlined for four to five months after tripling from February lows, meaning NEAR is taking market share but not growing revenue.
insights.speaker: Jamie Coutts
insights.so_what: Tells you exactly which metric to track for a NEAR re-rating: intents volume breaking out of its plateau, which requires sector-wide block-space demand to recover.
insights.quote: That means they're picking up market share, but they're not growing their revenue

insights.claim: The host argues that within three to five years governments will not tolerate how Hyperliquid is built or NEAR's transaction privacy because they want control, framing regulatory pressure as a medium-term risk to both despite short-term bullishness.
insights.speaker: host (Michael)
insights.so_what: A time-boxed regulatory risk on the exact names being recommended — argues for treating these as cycle trades rather than permanent holds.

insights.claim: Coutts says Zcash miner revenue is roughly 10x Bitcoin's on a relative basis, evidence the network is genuinely being used while Bitcoin struggles for block-space demand — yet he holds no position after exiting profitably this year, waiting to see how the protocol bug resolves.
insights.speaker: Jamie Coutts
insights.so_what: Contradicts the video title's implication of a held position; the actionable point is the fee-generation metric that makes Zcash structurally interesting when sentiment repairs.

insights.claim: Both speakers flag long-term concern on privacy coins from Western government crackdown, with the host noting European funds are prohibited from trading privacy coins like Dash and Monero, making them structurally uninvestable for regulated capital.
insights.speaker: host (Michael) and Jamie Coutts
insights.so_what: Caps the institutional bid for privacy coins regardless of fundamentals — a structural discount that will not close through adoption alone.

themes.theme: Positioning: max cash, bear-market breakouts and the re-entry trigger

insights.claim: Coutts says he is holding the highest amount of cash he has held in a long time and is only opportunistically adding to a couple of coins he likes, rather than adding meaningful risk.
insights.speaker: Jamie Coutts
insights.so_what: A senior crypto analyst's actual book is defensive despite a bullish long-term thesis — a sentiment datapoint on how positioned professionals currently are.
insights.quote: I'm holding the highest amount of cash that I have um for quite a long time

insights.claim: Coutts's quantitative work finds you can trade breakouts inside a bear-market regime but the odds of profitability are greatly diminished, and altcoin momentum in a bear market is a fraction of what it is when Bitcoin is in a bull regime — so trailing stops are mandatory.
insights.speaker: Jamie Coutts
insights.so_what: Regime-conditional expectancy: the same chart pattern has materially worse payoff in a bear tape, which argues for smaller size and tighter trailing exits.

insights.claim: Coutts rejects the view that recent altcoin outperformance proves decoupling from Bitcoin, calling it run-of-the-mill bear-market behaviour — pockets of outperformance appeared in 2022 and earlier bear markets too.
insights.speaker: Jamie Coutts
insights.so_what: Fades the 'altseason is starting' narrative built on Hyperliquid, Zcash and NEAR runs — NEAR has already given back about 50% of its move.

insights.claim: Coutts reports on-chain activity across fees, daily active users and the application layer is down on one-month, three-month, six-month and one-year bases, having peaked around July-August last year, with only pockets of improvement such as Hyperliquid fees and Morpho gaining on Aave in lending.
insights.speaker: Jamie Coutts
insights.so_what: The fundamental backdrop has not turned; a breakout in aggregate on-chain activity is the confirmation that would validate any price rally.

insights.claim: Coutts's re-entry checklist is a weekly-timeframe momentum shift, a liquidity-environment change including a dollar and real-yield rollover, and weekly RSI bullish divergences married with a momentum break — plus, ideally, altcoin dispersion driven by a break in the on-chain activity downtrend rather than price alone.
insights.speaker: Jamie Coutts
insights.so_what: A fully specified, checkable set of buy triggers an investor can monitor independently rather than guessing at his positioning.

insights.claim: Coutts warns most on-chain data is dollar-denominated and therefore contaminated by price — if Ethereum doubles, fee revenue doubles even with flat activity — so true signal requires metrics disentangled from price.
insights.speaker: Jamie Coutts
insights.so_what: A methodological edge: use unit-count metrics (transactions, users, active contracts) rather than USD-denominated fees when judging whether fundamentals are actually improving.
insights.quote: So the key is really to look for the onchain data that's disentangled from price as a true signal

insights.claim: The host observes multiple L1s are already building bases or breaking out against Bitcoin — naming Aave, Sui and Solana — and expects that when Bitcoin finds a short-term bottom, liquidity will rotate into those yield-bearing alternatives rather than into Bitcoin itself.
insights.speaker: host (Michael)
insights.so_what: A specific relative-value setup: long alt/BTC ratio pairs as the expression of a Bitcoin bottom, rather than long BTC outright.
